title: Your weekly seva
hook: choose one small regular service you can actually keep

segments.voice: Yesterday, haumai, the I that wants credit. Your line was serve, then forget it. Did you catch the wanting, and smile? Day one hundred three.

Every January, gyms fill up. New shoes, big plans, five mornings a week. By February, most of those people are gone. Not because they were lazy. Because the plan was too big to keep. Meanwhile there's a man who has walked the same two blocks every evening for eleven years, and he's the fittest person on the street. The small thing, kept, beats the big thing, dropped. The same is true of seva. This week you've tried an unseen kindness, the shoes, a dish, a tenth, a lesson taught. Today is the last day of seva week, and the question is simple: what will you actually keep?
screen: `THE JANUARY GYM.` → `TWO BLOCKS, ELEVEN YEARS.` → `WHAT WILL YOU ACTUALLY KEEP?`

segments.voice: In Sikh life, seva isn't mostly big moments. It's rhythm. Plenty of Sikh families have a weekly seva they've kept for years. The same Sunday shift in the langar kitchen. The same job cleaning the gurdwara's floors before the week begins. Driving the same elderly neighbor to the same appointment. Nobody's counting. It's just what Sunday is. Think back to the great example of the path: Amar Das, carrying water for Guru Angad. The story doesn't remember one heroic trip. It remembers that he did it every morning, before dawn, for years, until the carrying had changed him. That's what regular seva does. A single big act can feed haumai, the ego from yesterday: look what I did. A small act, repeated, gets boring to the ego, and that's the point. Around the hundredth time you wipe the same tables, there's nobody left to impress. There's only the table, and the people who'll eat there. So here's the wisdom Sikh teachers keep coming back to. Make it small. Make it specific. Make it regular. Not help more, but every Thursday I'll take my neighbor's bins out. Not give back, but the first Sunday of the month I'll cook at the gurdwara, or the food bank, or for the new parents down the hall. You can choose tan, man or dhan: your hands, your mind, your purse. You can choose something you'll never be thanked for. Just choose something you can keep. One seva, kept, does more than ten, dropped.
screen: `SEVA IS A RHYTHM.` · `AMAR DAS, EVERY MORNING, FOR YEARS.` · `SMALL ACTS BORE THE EGO.` · `SMALL, SPECIFIC, REGULAR.` · then, large: `ONE SEVA, KEPT.`

segments.voice: Settle, and breathe. Let the week's sevas pass in front of you. The unseen kindness. The shoes. The dish. The tenth. The thing you taught. Which one felt most like you? Now make it small enough to keep every week. Give it a day, and a time. Picture yourself doing it next week, and the week after, and in six months, when nobody remembers you started. If you pray, you can offer it. The bell holds the time.
Your weekly seva. One small, regular service, chosen to be kept, which does its quiet work over months and years.
Your line: one seva, kept. Today, write your weekly seva somewhere you'll see it, with its day. Tomorrow, kirtan begins. Day one hundred three.

howItsDone: Many Sikhs keep a regular seva, such as a weekly shift in the gurdwara langar or cleaning, and families often serve together on the same day each week.
